title: Customer Success vs. Account Management: Responsibilities, Handoffs, and Metrics
summary: Customer success and account management both support the continuing customer relationship, but teams often assign them different responsibilities.
body_markdown:
Customer success and account management both support the continuing customer relationship, but teams often assign them different responsibilities. Customer success commonly focuses on helping the customer achieve value. Account management commonly includes commercial continuity, renewals, and growth. The exact division varies by organisation.


The distinction becomes useful when it clarifies ownership. It becomes harmful when a customer is passed between teams because each believes the problem belongs to the other. Design around the customer’s journey and your actual staffing, not an idealised organisation chart.


## Define the outcomes before the titles


List the work that must happen after a sale: preserve the agreed goals, coordinate onboarding, resolve blockers, assess progress, prepare reviews, manage renewal decisions, and identify appropriate growth opportunities. Then assign the outcomes to roles.


An account manager may own several of these in a small company. A larger organisation may separate implementation, customer success, support, renewal operations, and expansion sales. Neither design is inherently correct. The important requirement is that every customer-facing commitment has a responsible owner.


Avoid assigning a person accountability for an outcome they cannot influence. A CSM cannot own a technical fix without access to the team that controls it. They can own communicating its status and escalating a missed commitment, while engineering or support owns resolution.


## A starting responsibility matrix


Work Accountable role to name Supporting roles to identify


Customer goals and success plan Relationship or success owner Customer sponsor, sales


Initial implementation Implementation owner Customer technical owner, CSM


Support issue resolution Support owner Product or engineering specialist


Customer communication during an issue Named relationship contact Support owner


Renewal process Commercial owner CSM, finance, procurement


Expansion qualification Agreed growth owner Relationship owner, product specialist


Replace role labels with real responsibilities in your company. The same person may occupy several rows. What matters is that the work does not become unowned when a department boundary is crossed.


## Where handoffs usually break


A sales-to-success handoff fails when the receiving team gets the contract but not the customer’s reasons for buying. It also fails when a promise made during the sale is omitted or softened into a vague note. The customer experiences the gap as “your team already knows this.”


A success-to-commercial handoff fails when a growth signal is passed along without context. “Interested in more seats” does not explain the use case, timing, decision-maker, or unresolved issues. The receiving person may make an aggressive approach that undermines trust.


A support-to-account handoff fails when notification is mistaken for acceptance. Mentioning the account manager does not establish who will update the customer or confirm that the issue is closed.


For each transition, define the minimum packet, the receiving owner’s acceptance, and a fallback if nobody accepts. Use the[handoff template](https://o11.ai/blog/sales-to-customer-success-handoff-template) to make those expectations visible.


## Align metrics without creating competing incentives


Metrics should reflect the work a role owns. Customer value milestones, completed onboarding, and resolution of outstanding commitments can help evaluate relationship work. Renewal and expansion measures help evaluate commercial outcomes, but attribution requires care.


Do not assume that every expansion proves customer success or that every non-renewal proves an individual failure. A customer can grow for reasons unrelated to the team’s work, or leave because of a strategic change. Review the evidence and context before turning a commercial result into a performance conclusion.


Shared metrics are helpful when teams genuinely share the process. For example, measure handoff acceptance quality and the number of customer repetitions caused by missing context. These reveal coordination problems that separate departmental dashboards can hide.


## An illustrative operating disagreement


Suppose a customer wants another business unit to join, but a critical onboarding task remains unfinished. Sales sees a qualified expansion opportunity. The CSM wants to delay the conversation until the existing team reaches value.


The answer is not automatically to suppress or accelerate the opportunity. Bring the two facts into one discussion. Ask whether the new unit has a distinct need, whether the current blocker affects it, and whether the customer actually wants to discuss scope now.


Document the agreed next step and who communicates it. The customer should receive one coherent plan, not competing messages from people optimising different internal metrics.


## A model for small teams


When one person owns both success and account management, separate the responsibilities in the workflow even if the role is combined. A customer review can include value, blockers, and future needs, but commercial decisions should be explicit rather than slipping into a support conversation unexpectedly.


Keep a shared account brief, a commitment register, and a clear renewal owner. Name a backup so that holidays or staff changes do not erase continuity. Review open commitments weekly instead of relying on one person’s memory.


Use the[book-of-business prioritisation guide](https://o11.ai/blog/account-management-prioritization) to allocate scarce attention. A simple, maintained process is better than a sophisticated responsibility model nobody follows.


## Where AI assistance belongs


AI can help prepare context and identify work that needs attention. It cannot resolve an organisational disagreement about who is accountable. Define ownership before automating the handoff, and require evidence before acting on a suggested commercial signal.
